stories.headline: Non-parties to compromise decree can appeal if rights are prejudiced: Supreme Court
stories.bodyText: New Delhi: The Supreme Court has clarified that a person who was not a party to a compromise decree is not automatically barred from filing an appeal under Section 96(3) read with Order XXIII Rules 3 and 3A of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908. However, non-party status alone does not give an unrestricted right to appeal. A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran ruled that such a person must first show a prima facie case that the decree harms their independent rights or interests. They must also seek and obtain leave from the appellate court, following established principles for appeals by strangers to the original suit. .'Distinguish consent from regret': Supreme Court warns, discharges man in rape case. The court stressed that appellate courts retain the discretion to grant interim protection while an appeal is pending, in order to safeguard the subject matter of the dispute. “Where a non-party demonstrates a prima facie case of prejudice, the court must balance the need to prevent irreparable loss or multiplicity of proceedings against the rights of the parties involved,” the bench said in its October 30, 2026 judgement. The ruling came in an appeal filed by Girishbhai Natwarlal Patel challenging a Gujarat High Court order. The high court had granted an ex parte ad interim injunction, later confirmed it after hearing both sides, allowed leave to appeal, and condoned an 11-year delay for respondents who were not parties to the original consent decree. The Supreme Court upheld the high court’s approach. It noted that limitation for non-parties cannot be calculated rigidly from the date of the decree. Courts must examine when the aggrieved person actually learnt, or could reasonably have learnt, of the decree and the resulting prejudice. Given the appellants’ non-party status, the delay was rightly condoned. The bench made it clear that the present proceedings were limited to examining the high court’s interim orders and grant of leave. It did not go into the merits of the challenge to the consent decree itself. On the facts, the court found that the circumstances surrounding the land transaction raised serious questions about how the appellant claimed title. Prima facie doubts existed over whether the legal heirs of Purshottam Punjabhai still held a transferable right. The appellant had also acted under a power of attorney from those heirs and appeared to have had close links with the original plaintiff society, including a reported stint as its chairman in 2002-03. .Anant Singh to surrender by December 1 in Dularchand Yadav murder case as Supreme Court directs. The high court was therefore justified in granting interim protection to preserve the subject matter. The continuation of the injunction followed a full hearing at which the appellant could contest the relief; it was not a mere extension of the earlier ex parte order, the bench said. Addressing the legal bar on appeals against consent decrees, the Supreme Court explained that Section 96(3) and Order XXIII Rules 3 and 3A create an estoppel only between the parties who actually compromised. A stranger who asserts an independent interest allegedly harmed by the decree stands on a different footing and cannot be treated as having consented to it. At the same time, leave to appeal is not automatic. An applicant must show that the decree prejudicially affects their rights; remote or indirect impact is not enough, the bench said. In the underlying dispute, a 1975 sale deed and subsequent mutation entries formed the backdrop. A 2012 specific-performance suit based on a 1996 agreement ended in a 2013 consent decree in favour of Geetagram Society. The decree was executed only years later, and a sale deed in the appellant’s favour was registered in 2022. Allegations that the appellant had acted for the original defendants under a 2012 power of attorney added to the concerns that warranted appellate scrutiny. These facts did not prove fraud or collusion at this stage, the court said, but they were sufficient to show that the respondents’ grievance was not frivolous. The high court therefore committed no error in granting leave, condoning delay, or protecting the subject matter. The Supreme Court directed the high court to hear and dispose of the main appeal within three months.

stories.headline: Trump administration to deport 150 Afghan refugees to Afghanistan via Pakistan
stories.bodyText:
The Trump administration is preparing to deport more than 150 Afghan immigrants and refugees to Taliban-controlled Afghanistan via Pakistan. The first deportation flight could take off as early as Monday.
The broader plan reportedly involves routing deportees through Pakistan because the United States has no diplomatic relations with the Taliban government in Afghanistan.
According to NBC News, Shawn VanDiver, president of San Diego-based advocacy group AfghanEvac, said at least 80 Afghans had recently been transferred to Louisiana from 34 ICE detention facilities across the United States. Of those, 19 were reportedly moved without legal representation.
Many of those facing deportation reportedly fled Afghanistan following the Taliban's return to power in 2021, including individuals whose family members had worked alongside US forces during the two-decade war.
Shawn warned that returning these individuals could expose them and their families to serious risks of persecution and retaliation.
"Some facing deportation are brothers and sons of men who served alongside US forces, families the Taliban already has every reason to target," VanDiver added.
A senior Trump administration official, speaking anonymously to NBC News, indicated that the potential consequences for Afghans facing deportation were not a major concern for the White House. “The administration’s position is, ‘These individuals do not have status in our country, therefore we don’t really care what happens to them,’” the official said.
The proposed removals come amid US president Donald Trump's broader immigration crackdown. Since returning to office, his administration has suspended refugee admissions, including those for Afghans who had sought protection in the United States following the 2021 withdrawal of US-led forces.
The policy marks a reversal of earlier efforts to provide refuge to Afghans fleeing Taliban rule and political instability.
The administration has also pursued third-country deportation arrangements, sending migrants to countries other than their countries of origin. Immigration lawyers and human rights advocates argue that such arrangements could circumvent international protections against returning asylum seekers to places where they may face persecution. The legality of these deportation policies is expected to come before the US Supreme Court in December.
VanDiver has called on Congress to intervene by passing legislation granting eligible Afghans temporary protected status (TPS), which would provide protection from deportation while conditions in Afghanistan remain dangerous.
Pakistan could also face complications if the proposed deportations proceed through its territory. Islamabad has already deported more than two million Afghan nationals since 2023.

briefs.headline: GSLV places next-generation navigation satellite NVS-03 into orbit
briefs.deck: The NVS-03, with a mission life of 12 years, is expected to restore the functioning of the NavIC constellation; satellite carries an indigenous atomic clock, along with procured atomic clocks
briefs.bodyText:
The Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV-F18) on Friday (October 30, 2026) successfully launched the NVS-03 satellite from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, according to the ISRO.
The GSLV-F18 with the NVS-03 satellite lifted off from the second launch pad of the spaceport and, 18 minutes later placed the satellite into the intended geosynchronous transfer orbit.
“The GSLV-F18 vehicle has successfully and precisely injected the NVS-03 satellite weighing 2250 kg in the intended elliptical orbit. Let me congratulate each and every team member of ISRO, industrial partners, academia for this outstanding accomplishment,” ISRO Chairman Dr. V. Narayanan said.
He added that the vehicle systems have performed as predicted and as expected.
The 2250 kg NVS-03 is the third satellite in the next-generation navigation satellite system envisaged for providing continuity of navigation services for the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS) series or the Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC).
According to the ISRO, the satellite carries an indigenous atomic clock, along with procured atomic clocks.
“It also includes L1 signal in addition to existing L5/S signals with coverage over India landmass and a region extending 1,500 km around Indian geopolitical boundary,” the ISRO said.
NavIC is India’s independent regional navigation satellite system designed to provide accurate position, navigation, and Timing (PNT) services to users in India as well as the region extending about 1,500 km beyond the Indian landmass, which is its primary service area.
The successful launch of the NVS-03, which will have a mission life of 12 years, is expected to restore the functioning of the NavIC constellation, which has been weakened due to repeated failures of atomic clocks and the ISRO’s inability to place its previous replacement satellite, NVS-02, in its intended orbit.
It can be recalled that earlier this year, on March 13, the last functioning atomic clock aboard IRNSS-1F had stopped working.
The ISRO Chairman said that with the success of the mission, the NavIC constellation is restored to the minimum operational configuration with four satellites.
“Already three satellites are successfully working in orbit, with this satellite we will have four satellites and restore the PNT services of the country. As you know, the NavIC constellation is a strategic national asset that provides the nation independent access to PNT services. It is also used for civilian applications like real-time tracking of trains along with tracking of vehicles and shipping vessels. It is an important component of the One Nation One Time Project,” the ISRO Chairman said.
Friday’s (October 30, 2026) launch is only the third mission to be launched by ISRO in 2026, after the PSLV-C62 mission carrying the EOS-N1 Earth observation satellite on January 12, 2026, and the EOS-05 aboard the GSLV-F17 on September 4. While the PSLV-C62 mission was a failure, the GSLV-F17 mission was a success.
“This mission was accomplished with the least turnaround time of just 56 days between successive GSLV missions,” Dr. Narayanan said.
PM Modi congratulates ISRO
Prime Minister Narendra Modi congratulated ISRO for the successful launch of GSLV-F18 carrying NVS-03.
“This mission marks an important step in strengthening NavIC, our indigenous satellite navigation system,” Mr. Modi said in a post on X. The dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists continue to make our nation proud, he added.

briefs.headline: Flavio Bolsonaro says he left Brazil because he is the victim of 'persecution'
briefs.deck: "The persecution began even sooner than I imagined," Mr. Bolsonaro said during an Instagram livestream in which he discussed his decision to flee after his Brazilian passports were cancelled as part of a money laundering investigation
briefs.bodyText:
Former conservative presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro said Friday (October 30, 2026) that he fled Brazil to the United States because he was a victim of "persecution" in his country.
Mr. Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday's (October 25) election runoff to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, secretly left Brazil on Tuesday (October 27) and arrived in Florida aboard a private jet on Wednesday (October 28) after travelling through Argentina and Ecuador.
"The persecution began even sooner than I imagined," the senator said during an Instagram livestream in which he discussed his decision to flee after his Brazilian passports were cancelled as part of a money laundering investigation.
In the video, he recounted how police informed him on Monday that his passports were being revoked as he left a visit to his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest.
Also Read: Flavio Bolsonaro reaches U.S., say reports citing sources
"With tears in his eyes, he told me: 'You know where they're going with this, don't you?'" he said of his father.
"I told him: 'Dad, I know... Now I know what I have to do,'" he recounted.
Although he gave no details of how he left the country, he said he and his wife made the decision "without anyone knowing" and urged people not to "point the finger at anyone."
U.S. President Donald Trump and Argentine President Javier Milei are under pressure to explain the involvement of the United States and Argentina in the senator's escape.
"I didn't leave Brazil; I left for Brazil," Flavio Bolsonaro said, alleging that Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes had made false accusations against him.
He also suggested there had been irregularities in the runoff, comparing them to "handball goals" that were not disallowed by VAR, without detailing what those irregularities might have been.
He also predicted that the economy would "go bust" under Lula and said he was willing to run for president again: "I'm not talking about 2030, I'm talking about before then."

briefs.headline: U.S. imprisons two Chinese nationals for spying
briefs.deck: The U.S. Department of Justice said the men had carried out clandestine intelligence activities in the United States that included facilitating "dead drop" cash payments in exchange for information related to the national security of the United States
briefs.bodyText:
Two Chinese men who admitted trying to recruit U.S. military service members to spy for Beijing were imprisoned in California on Friday (October 30, 2026).
Liren Lai and Yuance Chen were ordered to serve 30 months in a federal lockup and to undergo three years of supervised release after pleading guilty to acting on the orders of China's Ministry of State Security.
The U.S. Department of Justice said the men had carried out clandestine intelligence activities in the United States that included facilitating "dead drop" cash payments in exchange for information related to the national security of the United States.
They also gathered information on U.S. military personnel and installations and attempted to recruit intelligence assets within the U.S. military.
"Let this sentencing serve as a clear warning: If you attempt to jeopardise the safety and security of our service members, our citizens, or our nation, justice will find you," said Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division.
Lai, who arrived in the U.S. on a tourist visa, recruited Chen — a permanent resident — into the scheme and initially served as an intermediary between Chen and intelligence officers, until Chen was able to receive his orders directly from his handler.
The DoJ said the two men had been working since at least May 2021 for the branch of the Chinese government responsible for conducting foreign intelligence and counterintelligence operations.
They were arrested in June 2025. Both men pleaded guilty to conspiracy to act as agents of a foreign government without prior notification to the Attorney General and acting as agents of a foreign government without prior notification over the following months.

briefs.headline: Kansas teacher's daily affirmations spread to other classrooms
briefs.deck: An elementary teacher in Kansas has implemented positive affirmations at the end of each school day. This practice has spread across various grades, enhancing students' sense of belonging and value. While affirmations alone do not replace effective teaching methods, they contribute to a supportive classroom atmosphere. Parents can also foster encouragement in their children by acknowledging their…
briefs.bodyText:
Someone truly said that a teacher can change a thousand lives. One such example is an elementary school teacher from Kansas, who came up with a simple idea of ending each school day with children repeating positive affirmations. What began as a small classroom routine soon caught on, inspiring other teachers across the school to adopt the practice.
At a time when conversations around children’s education often revolve around academic performance, grades, dress codes and whatnot, this simple initiative offers a gentle reminder that just a few words of encouragement can become an opportunity for children to recognise their own strengths and leave school feeling valued and with a sense of belonging.
How one teacher's idea spread across the school
Image representation of the teacher's Support to the students (source: Canva) 
Tyler Richards, a first-grade teacher at Rex Elementary School in Haysville, Kansas, has been receiving appreciation for his simple approach to ending the school day. Before leaving the classroom, his young students repeat positive affirmations, including phrases such as “I am kind” and “I can do hard things”.
The idea might feel simple and ordinary at first, but its purpose goes beyond having children memorise a few encouraging sentences. 
By repeating these words together, students get an opportunity to remind themselves that they can be kind, face challenges and approach new situations with confidence. Moreover, this small gesture creates a lasting bond between students and their teacher, allowing students to trust and depend on their teachers even outside academics.
The idea soon caught the attention of the school’s principal, Shane Paulus, who appreciated the way it helped children feel welcomed and valued. Speaking about the practice, Paulus told KSN News that it was a good way for students to feel loved and appreciated before heading home and to end their day on a positive note.
What makes the story particularly heartwarming is how quickly the idea travelled beyond Richards' own classroom. Teachers across different grades at Rex Elementary began introducing similar practices, allowing more children to participate in the daily exercise.
According to the report by Good News Network, students themselves have also started taking ownership of the initiative by suggesting new ways to put the practice into action. This response suggests that the routine has become more than something children are instructed to do. Instead, they are beginning to own it as something of their own.
Why positive affirmations can matter during childhood
Positive affirmations (Image- Canva)
Childhood is a period when children gradually develop an understanding of themselves, their abilities and their relationships with others. Along the way, they encounter new experiences, make mistakes, struggle with unfamiliar tasks and learn how to navigate friendships. The way adults respond to these encounters shapes how children view their own capabilities.
Positive affirmations not only remind children of their own strengths but also assure them that the adults around them trust them, value them and consider them individuals. These affirmations remind them that there is more to life than failures. For a young child, even a seemingly simple challenge can feel like the end of the world. Whether it is starting a new semester or making new friends, these messages encourage children to focus on positive aspects of themselves.
Of course, repeating affirmations is not a substitute for good teaching, emotional and personal guidance, or addressing the difficulties a child may be experiencing. Children also need adults who listen to them, acknowledge their feelings and help them work through problems. Encouraging words are most meaningful when they are reinforced by everyday experiences in which children feel respected and supported.
A small classroom habit with a larger message
One of the significant aspects of this initiative is its emphasis on making children feel that they belong. For young students, school is not only where they learn academic skills. It is also where they build relationships with teachers, interact with classmates and begin to understand how they fit into a larger community.
Richards has emphasised the importance of creating a safe place for children. Children spend a significant amount of their day at school. This is an important part of the story because a child's experience of school extends beyond what happens during a lesson.
When children feel comfortable asking questions, making mistakes and seeking help, they have more opportunities to participate in the classroom. A welcoming environment cannot be created through affirmations alone, but small gestures of reassurance can form part of a broader effort to build that environment.
There is also a lesson here for parents and caregivers. Encouragement does not always have to come in the form of elaborate praise or rewards. Reminding children that they can learn from mistakes, that kindness matters and that asking for help is acceptable can become part of everyday conversations at home. The most important thing parents often forget is that their children are also individuals with their own personalities and emotions and must be treated as such.
Ultimately, Richards' initiative is a reminder that teaching involves more than helping children understand what is written in their textbooks. It also involves creating an environment in which they feel seen, supported and encouraged to grow. Sometimes, it is a small idea that makes a big difference.

briefs.headline: Alaska Airlines to cut 200 jobs as Iran war-driven fuel costs threaten $700 million loss
briefs.bodyText:
Alaska Air Group will eliminate around 200 non-contract positions as soaring fuel prices and geopolitical tensions linked to the Iran war put pressure on its finances, with the airline warning it could suffer losses of up to $700 million this year.
The job cuts, announced on Friday, signal how the fuel-price shock triggered by the Iran war is beginning to affect employment in the US aviation industry, with carriers already raising airfares and scaling back expansion plans to offset higher operating costs.
In a memo to employees, Chief Executive Ben Minicucci said the company could report an adjusted pretax loss of as much as $700 million in 2026 if current conditions persist. This would mark its first adjusted pretax loss outside the Covid-19 pandemic since 2003, Reuters reported.
"We must return to the financial discipline that has long been a key competitive advantage," Minicucci said, adding that overhead expenses had "grown at a disproportionate rate to revenue" in recent years.
The reductions will affect less than 1% of Alaska Air's approximately 32,500 employees. These include 125 positions in Washington state and 48 in Hawaii. 
The company said no frontline or non-management jobs would be eliminated.
Affected employees will have November 13 as their last working day but will continue receiving pay through December 31, along with severance and other support, according to the memo.
Expansion plans face financial pressure
The Seattle-based airline is pursuing an ambitious expansion into premium and international travel following its acquisition of Hawaiian Airlines. Its strategy includes investments in premium cabins, loyalty programmes and new international routes, with plans to expand its long-haul network from Seattle.
Minicucci said the company would continue investing in its fleet, customer experience and network despite tightening spending elsewhere.

briefs.headline: 'India's self-reliance in critical technologies': PM Modi on Isro's NVS-03 success
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday congratulated Indian Space Research Organisation (
ISRO
) scientists and engineers following the successful launch of the GSLV-F18 mission carrying the NVS-03 navigation satellite, saying the mission would strengthen India's indigenous satellite navigation system, 
NavIC
.
In a post on X, PM Modi said, "Congratulations to our scientists and engineers at ISRO on the successful launch of GSLV-F18 carrying NVS-03.
Also read: Success launch of navigation sat NVS-03 with desi atomic clock will make NaVIC up & running, and give military strategic independence
This mission marks an important step in strengthening NavIC, our indigenous satellite navigation system. Equipped with enhanced capabilities, NVS-03 will further our pursuit of self-reliance in critical technologies and support navigation services that benefit our people.
The dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists continue to make our nation proud."
The successful launch is expected to strengthen India's strategic autonomy by helping restore the operational capabilities of NavIC, India's indigenous alternative to global navigation systems such as the US-operated GPS and Russia's GLONASS.
The NVS-03 satellite carries an indigenously developed atomic clock, alongside imported atomic clocks, marking an important step towards reducing India's dependence on foreign technologies for satellite-based navigation. 
Atomic clocks provide highly precise time signals that are essential for determining location, navigation and timing.
NavIC, which was originally designed around a seven-satellite constellation, had been operating with only three active satellites, below the minimum requirement of four satellites for standalone positioning services. This had limited its use for critical applications, including military navigation, precision positioning and coordination of naval assets.
An operational NavIC constellation is particularly important for India's armed forces, which require reliable Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) signals for missile guidance, precision-guided weapons, troop movement, combat aircraft and naval operations.
Dependence on foreign navigation networks can pose strategic vulnerabilities during conflicts, as access to such services could potentially be restricted or disrupted. India experienced the limitations of relying on foreign satellite navigation systems during the 1999 Kargil war.
With NVS-03, India aims to strengthen the availability of indigenous navigation services for both civilian and strategic applications. NavIC is designed to provide coverage across India and up to 1,500 km beyond its geographical boundaries.

The original NavIC constellation comprised seven satellites supported by a network of ground stations operating round the clock. Three satellites were placed in geostationary orbit, while four were placed in inclined geosynchronous orbits.
However, the constellation's operational strength declined over time as ageing satellites could not be replaced as planned. The launch of NVS-02 on January 29, 2025, also failed to deliver the intended results after a pyro valve signal loss in the engine prevented the satellite from reaching its designated orbit.
The successful deployment of NVS-03 is expected to address some of these operational limitations and strengthen India's efforts to establish an independent satellite navigation capability.

stories.headline: Cop, bizman, contractor, 2 advocates: The 5 Bengaluru friends killed in Uttarakhand chopper crash
stories.deck: A police inspector from Bengaluru and four friends died in a helicopter crash while on a pilgrimage. They had taken off from Badrinath for Dehradun when contact was lost shortly after takeoff. The helicopter was later located with smoke rising from the wreckage in the Hathi Parvat area. Recovery efforts were hindered by darkness and difficult terrain, delaying body retrieval.
stories.bodyText:
BENGALUURU/CHAMOLI: A 44-year-old police inspector from Bengaluru city and his four friends who were on a pilgrimage to Badrinath died in a helicopter crash in Uttarakhand on an overcast Friday after the chopper lost contact within minutes after takeoff. The copter pilot was among the dead.
According to sources, the five had reached Uttarakhand on Wednesday and taken a chopper ride between Badarinath and Dehradun.
The deceased have been identified as Arun Salunke, HS Nataraj, 51, K Sudheer, 39, Shankar Gowda, 34 and B Pratap Gowda, 41 (all from Karnataka). The dead pilot was identified as Capt Himanshu Sabharwal, 48, from Delhi.
The helicopter lost contact in less than two minutes after taking off from Badrinath. “The helicopter (VT-HCX) departed from Badrinath for Sahastradhara (Dehradun) at 1.12pm. At 1.14pm, contact with the helicopter was lost near Joshimath and information regarding its disappearance was received from an Army post,” a source said. The District Emergency Operations Centre said the helicopter was spotted by the Army’s Signal Centre team in the Hathi Parvat area and “smoke was seen rising from the helicopter, and it was observed losing altitude rapidly”.
According to sources, the bodies were found in the wreckage in Chai village. Due to darkness and the difficult terrain, the bodies will be brought back from the crash site on Saturday.
Who were the 5 killed?
Arun Salunke, attached to the special inquiry squad with the Central Crime Branch and from Artal village in Athani taluk of Belagavi district, was in the news when he booked an IAS officer from Andhra Pradesh, Vikas Marmat, and his friends on alleged charges of misbehaving with and abusing cops on the intervening night of Oct 10 and Oct 11. The incident had taken place when a team led by Salunke entered a night club to inspect whether liquor was being served to underage revellers.
Nataraj was a businessman from Huliyurdurga in Tumakuru; Pratap, a civil contractor, was from Jakkur in the city; Sudheer K, from Nagarabavi, and Shankar Gowda, from Tumakuru, were advocates.
According to a statement from the Karnataka govt, the CM’s office and the relief commissioner are coordinating with their counterparts in Uttarakhand to facilitate shifting the mortal remains to Karnataka soon.

stories.headline: Retired IAS officer issues legal notice to Karnataka police over late-night firecracker bursting
stories.deck: He alleges failure to enforce the Supreme Court’s ban on bursting sound-emitting firecrackers between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m; says he has respiratory ailments
stories.bodyText:
With the late-night bursting of firecrackers continuing despite repeated complaints, 85-year-old retired IAS officer M.G. Devasahayam has served a legal notice on the State Director-General and Inspector-General of Police, the Bengaluru City Police Commissioner and police officials at Banaswadi police station, alleging failure to enforce the Supreme Court’s ban on bursting sound-emitting firecrackers between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.
Mr. Devasahayam, who lives in Lingarajapuram, said he suffers from respiratory ailments and has accused the police of failing to take action despite being repeatedly alerted to the bursting of loud firecrackers almost every night.
In the legal notice dated October 30, he has given the officials three days to ensure enforcement of noise pollution regulations.
The notice states that the disturbance has continued for several months, with firecrackers being burst after 10 p.m., mostly continuing past midnight and, at times, until the early hours of the morning. It says repeated exposure to high-intensity noise, smoke and fumes from the crackers has affected Mr. Devasahayam’s health. The notice also points to the impact on other residents, particularly senior citizens, infants and those with health conditions.
According to the notice, Mr. Devasahayam first emailed the City Police Commissioner on August 12, bringing the disturbance to his attention and seeking urgent intervention. The complaint was also marked to the Chief Secretary, who forwarded it to the Police Commissioner and the Member Secretary of the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board on the same day. The Chief Secretary forwarded it again on September 1. However, despite further reminders on August 16 and 27, the nuisance continued without any effective intervention.
He then sent several messages to the Police Commissioner and the Banaswadi Station House Officer. The notice states that the Station House Officer telephoned Mr. Devasahayam following one of the complaints and later visited his residence with two Assistant Sub-Inspectors. The officers promised him that those responsible would be identified and stringent action taken, and that the Supreme Court’s directions would be enforced.
However, the noise continued despite the assurance. Mr. Devasahayam continued to complain to the police and also sent representations to the Director-General and Inspector-General of Police. On another night, loud drum-beating continued until midnight. As recently as October 24-25, loud blasts continued until 5 a.m., the notice said.
The notice cites the Supreme Court’s July 18, 2005, judgment in In Re: Noise Pollution (V), which bans sound-emitting firecrackers between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. It also prohibits the use of drums, trumpets and other sound-producing instruments and amplifiers during these hours, except in public emergencies. The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, and a Karnataka Government circular dated May 10, 2022, also direct the authorities, including the police, to enforce the restrictions.
Commissioner responsible
The notice says the Police Commissioner is responsible for enforcing noise standards and alleges that the police have failed in their duty despite repeated complaints.
The retired IAS officer has asked the police to step up night patrolling, identify those bursting firecrackers after 10 p.m. and take action against them, including filing FIRs where necessary. He has also sought directions to police officers to enforce the ban, ensure that complaints are acted upon. He has also demanded an inquiry into why the police did not act on his complaints and a report on the action taken.
This is the second instance of citizens approaching the authorities over firecracker-related noise pollution. Recently, a group of citizens had served legal notices on several senior State government officials and the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board over the repeated bursting of firecrackers during the Ganesha festival, saying it had caused considerable distress.

stories.headline: Bengaluru needs long-term master plan for water, roads and sewerage: KBG
stories.deck: The Minister said a uniform policy would hold agencies excavating roads accountable for restoration, with clear standards, cost recovery and penalties for violations.
stories.bodyText:
Greater Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda has directed officials to prepare a comprehensive, long-term master plan to provide drinking water, road connectivity, and underground drainage infrastructure across the Bengaluru Urban district, including areas beyond the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) limits.
Mr. Gowda chaired the fourth Executive Committee meeting of the Bengaluru Development Authority at Vikas Soudha on Friday. He said infrastructure projects must be taken up in phases with clearly defined timelines, keeping pace with the city’s rapid expansion.
The Minister said a uniform policy would hold agencies excavating roads accountable for restoration, with clear standards, cost recovery and penalties for violations.
He also stressed the need to prioritise scientific treatment and reuse of sewage to improve water security. He cited the KC Valley, HN Valley, and Vrishabhavathi Valley projects, which supply treated wastewater to lakes across neighbouring districts.
Further, he directed the BMTC to introduce GPS-enabled feeder buses within a 2 to 3 km radius of Metro stations, with fixed routes. Plans are also under way to integrate private auto-rickshaw and taxi services with the BMTC 2.0 app, which already facilitates combined ticket bookings for Metro and BMTC services.
The government has also approved nine additional fire stations across the five municipal corporations under the GBA, taking the proposed network beyond the existing 20, he said.

stories.headline: I am eager to learn North Karnataka's folk music: Ricky Kej
stories.bodyText:
For 
Ricky Kej
, the excitement of making music lies in not knowing exactly how he is going to pull it off. The Grammy-winning composer, who has spent years taking Indian sounds to global audiences, is now preparing to enter a different musical landscape with filmmaker Sagar Puranik’s upcoming Kannada film, rooted in cultures of North Karnataka. In a chat with Bangalore Times, he talks about his fascination with folk traditions, the responsibility of telling stories through music and why he continues to seek out projects that challenge him
‘If I’m not scared, it’s not a project worth doing’
Ricky is clear about what draws him to a project. It is rarely the prospect of commercial success or the expectation of an audience. “For me, if I’m doing something just for the money, or because an audience demands it from me, that is not exciting. I always want to push the boundaries of what music can do. Every project I do has to include something completely new that I have never done before. If I start a project and I’m not really scared about how I’m going to pull it off, then I feel it’s not a project worth doing for me,” he says.
That uncertainty is part of what excites him about the upcoming Kannada film. “I’m not an expert when it comes to folk music from North Karnataka. 
But I have an absolute thirst to learn about it,” he says. More importantly, he does not intend to simply collect sounds and recreate them in the studio. “I would love to collaborate with musicians who have been practising this music their entire lives and come from a lineage of that tradition. It’s not about me learning everything and doing it myself. I want to work with them,” he shares.
‘Music can change how you see something’
Ricky’s approach to film scoring is shaped by a question that goes beyond melody: what does the music make the audience feel about what they are watching? “Music highlights emotions. Sometimes it is not even heard consciously, but it is felt. Even if an audience knows nothing about a particular musical form, they will subconsciously recognise when something does not feel authentic,” he says.
‘I want every project to challenge me as an artiste’
While the film marks an interesting new direction, Ricky is far from slowing down elsewhere. His India tour, meanwhile, has been postponed amid security concerns and uncertainty surrounding protests and permissions. For an artist who moves between orchestral compositions, collaborations and culturally rooted projects, the variety seems to be the point rather than a balancing act. “I love experimenting with music and collaborating with people. I want to constantly challenge myself,” he says.

briefs.headline: Seven packaged drinking water units closed for violations in Karnataka
briefs.deck: 102 units inspected in two days; 69 water samples collected for laboratory analysis
briefs.bodyText:
Karnataka’s Food Safety and Drug Administration has closed seven packaged drinking water units across Karnataka for major violations, including severe unhygienic conditions, operating without mandatory licences and non-cooperation with inspection teams, as part of a Statewide special inspection drive.
Officials also seized 82 cases of one-litre packaged drinking water bottles, valued at ₹7,380, from M.S. Food and Beverages in Devanahalli taluk of Bengaluru Rural district after detecting labelling defects.
As many as 102 packaged drinking water units were inspected between October 29 and 30, 69 water samples collected for laboratory analysis and issued notices to 53 food business operators (FBOs) for various violations.
On the second day of the drive, officials inspected 57 units and collected 37 samples for testing. Notices were issued to 29 units for violations, including unhygienic conditions, absence of medical certificates for food handlers, labelling defects, non-availability of water analysis reports and lack of mandatory pest control certificates.
Among the units closed were S.P. Food and Beverages in Hassan district, Avanti Industries in Bengaluru Urban district and Sai Ram Food Beverages in Bidar district for severe unhygienic conditions.
Om Shakthi Minerals in Bengaluru Urban, Nandi Food and Beverages in Kalaburagi and Dalia Beverages in Mysuru Rural were shut down for operating without the mandatory Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) licence. Nandi Food and Beverages was also found to be maintaining unhygienic conditions.
Aqua Refresh Packaged Drinking Water Unit in Kalaburagi district was closed following non-cooperation during inspection and investigation.
The samples collected during the inspections have been sent to government food laboratories to assess their quality and compliance with prescribed food safety standards.
The department said the special inspection drive would continue across the State and warned that stringent legal action would be initiated against packaged drinking water units found violating the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the rules framed under it.

briefs.headline: Karnataka’s milk price hike draws flak for impact on budget and nutrition
briefs.deck: Experts warn of increased household expenses and reduced access to essential nutrition, particularly for low-income families
briefs.bodyText:
The State government's announcement of a hike in milk prices by ₹8 per litre, which will come into effect on Sunday (November 1), has been criticised by experts and the public alike for its impact on budget and nutrition.
Dhananjaya Padmanabhachar, convener of the Income Tax Payers’ Forum, Bengaluru, said, “Since 2023, milk prices in Karnataka have increased by ₹15 per litre. According to my calculations, this represents a 38.5% increase. Even the salaries of people across various professions have not increased by 30% over the past three to four years. Some have also lost their jobs in private companies as artificial intelligence and other technologies replace human resources. How are such people expected to manage when the prices of essential commodities like milk continue to rise?”
He said, “Milk prices have been increased four times since 2023, including the latest hike. The price was increased by ₹3 per litre in August 2023. In another revision, ₹2 was added to the price per packet, along with an increase in quantity by 50 ml, taking a one-litre packet to 1.05 litres. On April 1, 2025, the price was increased by another ₹4 per litre. The latest increase is ₹8 per litre.”
Rising health risks
Sylvia Karpagam, public health expert and nutritionist, said that the increase in milk prices would disproportionately affect the working class, particularly daily-wage labourers such as construction workers, domestic workers and security guards.
“The government has already stopped providing eggs under the midday meal scheme, while meat has become increasingly expensive. With milk also becoming less affordable, we are likely to see a rise in stunting and other nutritional deficiencies among children and women in the State,” Ms. Karpagam said.
She added that a UNICEF report released in 2025 highlighted nutritional deficiencies among the State’s population, including deficiencies in vitamin B12, zinc, calcium and vitamin A.
“Foods rich in essential nutrients and proteins should be subsidised by the government. Instead, they are becoming inaccessible to the working class,” she said.
Dr. Sylvia said that the government should procure milk directly from farmers and make it available at subsidised rates to people below the poverty line. “People are left with cereals as their primary source of sustenance. Consequently, we can expect healthcare costs to rise, along with an increase in illnesses among children,” she added.
Low-wage workers hit
Citing the example of garment workers, Prathiba R., president of the Garment and Textile Workers Union (GATWU), said, “While the prices of milk and other essential commodities continue to rise, garment workers’ monthly salaries have remained stagnant at ₹13,500 for the past 10 years. In a family of five to six members, how can the government expect workers earning such low wages to afford these rising costs? Essential commodities should be made more affordable and accessible rather than becoming increasingly expensive.”
T.M. Rudramurthy, general secretary of the Auto Rickshaw Drivers Union, expressed disappointment with both the Union and State governments, saying that rising prices had become a routine occurrence, leaving ordinary people with little time or means to protest.
“Price rise has become the norm. The common man does not have the time to protest against the government. If we take part in a protest, we lose a day’s wages,” he said. He added that auto LPG prices had increased from ₹66 to ₹77 per litre as of Friday (October 30).

briefs.headline: Two friends, same police batch: Karnataka loses second officer in two months
briefs.bodyText:
A helicopter crash in Uttarakhand on Friday claimed the life of Karnataka police inspector Arun Salunke, making him the second police officer from the State to die in an accident in another State within two months.
Among those killed in the crash with him were Pratap Gowda, Shankar Gowda, Sudheer K., and H.S. Natraja. They were together on Char Dham yatra pilgrimage.
Mr. Salunke was an inspector with the Special Inquiry Wing of the Bengaluru Central Crime Branch (CCB). The Police Department sources described him as a “no-nonsense” officer with a calm demeanor.
On August 28, Ravi K.B., a cybercrime investigator, died in a bus accident in Madhya Pradesh. Both Mr. Ravi and Mr. Salunke belonged to the same batch of police officers who joined the service in 2007. What makes the tragedy even more heartbreaking is that both were part of the same close-knit group of friends.
As news of the helicopter crash broke, the social media accounts of several police officers filled with prayers and messages hoping that the reports were not true. Minutes later, when the deaths were confirmed, the posts quickly changed to photographs of Mr. Ravi and Mr. Salunke together.
One picture, however, was common across several posts: a screenshot of Mr. Salunke’s heartfelt social media post on August 28, mourning the death of his friend Ravi.
Mr. Salunke hailed from Aratal village in Belagavi district but had settled in Bengaluru for nearly two decades. He is survived by his wife and two children. His father and brothers reside in Aratal.
Vasanth Kumar, inspector of the Mahadevapura police station, said Mr. Salunke was a gentleman. “About 10 of us from the 2007 batch of 365 officers were very close, including Salunke and Ravi. We have lost two of them, and for many of us, it is a personal loss,” he told The Hindu.
A senior officer who had worked with Mr. Salunke said that he was quick-thinking and had a knack for identifying connections and unearthing leads swiftly.
Mr. Salunke had led a team that busted a betting racket during the Indian Premier League (IPL) 2026 earlier this year. He was also the complainant in a case in which an IAS officer from Andhra Pradesh allegedly assaulted and threatened police personnel during a late-night inspection earlier this month.
Family sources said Mr. Salunke had cleared a central services examination in 2007 and served in Delhi for some time. He later cleared the police recruitment examination and returned to Karnataka. He served in Bengaluru in various capacities and had also been posted in Tumakuru district. He had left for Uttarakhand on a trip with his friends last week.
Pratap Gowda hailed from Bachihalli in Sakleshpur. A contractor and businessman, he had been living in Bengaluru for several years. He is survived by his wife and two children. He was also inclined towards entering politics. According to his friends, he had recently joined the Congress and was interested in contesting the upcoming Zilla Panchayat elections from the Yeslur constituency in Sakleshpur taluk.

briefs.headline: Youth theatre fest brings stories of identity and grief to Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Young performers will get a chance to shine on stage at the fourth edition of Connections India in Bengaluru from November 4 to 6. Six schools and organisations will take part in the two-day theatre festival, presenting six performances alongside a range of workshops. The plays will explore themes such as friendship, identity, grief, climate change, and the decisions that shape young lives.
‘Being in a room together is what makes theatre special’
Bruce Guthrie, director of the National Centre for the Performing Arts (NCPA), says Bengaluru’s vibrant theatre culture offers an opportunity to build lasting relationships with schools, teachers, and young students.
“Young people have access to an enormous range of storytelling through their phones and screens. Theatre offers something immediate: being in a room together, listening, experimenting, and creating something that depends on everyone’s contribution,” he says, adding, “They should have the space to ask questions, make creative choices and discover what they want to communicate to an audience.”
‘Young people deserve stories that reflect their lives’
Five plays will be staged on friendship, identity, grief, climate change and social inequality to spotlight issues that shape young people’s lives and the world they are growing up in. 
“These are issues that affect their lives and shape the world they are growing up in. They deserve plays that recognise that complexity, with compelling characters, humour, uncertainty and room for different interpretations,” says Bruce.
“Relevance also comes through the rehearsal process. We want students to explore what a story means to them, recognise something from their own lives, and see a character’s experience challenge their assumptions. The aim is to give young people stories they can engage with honestly, and the confidence to bring their own understanding to the work,” he emphasises.

briefs.headline: Lured by quick profits, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1.1 crore to stock-trading scammers
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Lured by promises of hefty returns from stock trading through a WhatsApp group, a 51-year-old private firm employee lost over Rs 1.1 crore after investing in a fraudulent trading application called ISL MAX. The fraudsters displayed fake profits to gain his confidence, persuaded him to transfer money to multiple bank accounts and repeatedly demanded more deposits, but he was unable to withdraw his funds.
Prabhu
 (name changed), a resident of BDA Layout on Hennur Main Road, told police he received a WhatsApp message on Aug 13 from an unknown ISL 1-on-1 Group. Fraudsters posing as members shared messages about stock trading, claiming that those interested could earn huge profits by investing in stocks and trading regularly. Fraudsters shared fake screenshots of the profits earned and messages showing amounts credited to their bank accounts.
Convinced by their claims, Prabhu agreed to participate in trading. The fraudsters sent him a link to download an application called ISL MAX. After opening the application, he was asked to enter his personal and banking details to complete the identification and verification process.
The fraudsters subsequently began sending him bank account details through WhatsApp, instructing him to transfer money to the accounts for trading. 
He was told to buy stocks recommended through the app and sell them the following day after the market opened.
On Sept 2, Prabhu transferred Rs 25,000 from his account. The app showed profits after the deposit, reinforcing his belief that the trading scheme was genuine. He continued transferring money between Sept 2 and Oct 25: a total of Rs 1,12,37,437 through his four accounts.
However, when Prabhu tried to withdraw funds, he was unable to do so. The fraudsters kept insisting that he deposit more money, offering different excuses whenever he sought to access his investments.
Realising he had been duped, Prabhu approached East cybercrime police on Oct 26, and a case was registered under Information Technology Act and BNS Section 318 (cheating).

briefs.headline: New social media friend steals Bengaluru woman’s gold chain while she was sleeping in hotel room
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A casual outing with a new social media acquaintance turned into an expensive affair for a 27-year-old private firm employee after the man stole her 12-gram gold chain and pendant while she was asleep.
Sarita
 (name changed), staying in a paying guest accommodation near Hope Farm, Whitefield, told police she got to know the man, identified as 
Karthik
, on 
Snapchat
 around 20 days ago. After exchanging messages for a few days, the two decided to meet.
They checked into a hotel in Marathahalli around 10:15pm on Oct 24. They partied for some time, and before going to sleep, Sarita kept her gold chain and pendant on a table in the room.
When she woke up at 7:20am the next day, Karthik was missing, along with the jewellery. Shocked, Sarita tried to reach him on the phone but could not connect. She filed a complaint with HAL police the same day seeking his identification and recovery of her jewellery.

briefs.headline: ‘We lost a dear one’: Bengaluru cops mourn inspector Arun Salunke’s death in chopper crash
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Shock, disbelief and grief have gripped city police, particularly the 2007-batch officers, following the death of inspector Arun Salunke in a helicopter accident near Joshimath, Uttarakhand, Friday. For his batchmates, the loss has reopened painful memories of another colleague’s death just two months ago.
“We are unable to come to terms with Arun’s death. We’ve lost two inspectors in just over two months. Earlier, inspector Ravi KB died in an accident in Madhya Pradesh on Aug 28 while on official duty. Both officers belong to the 2007 batch. We don’t know what curse has befallen us,” a batchmate told 
TOI
.
The grief is particularly intense as colleagues remember Arun not just as a fellow officer, but as a close friend with big dreams for his family. He is survived by two children, whose future and education were always on his mind. “He would often tell us he wanted to provide his children with a good education and see them become top bureaucrats — IAS or IPS officers,” the batchmate said.
For another batchmate, the shock came soon after he woke up. Having been on duty the previous night, he got some rest Friday. When he woke up around 3.30pm, the first news he heard was of Arun’s death. 
“I was in shock for nearly 15 minutes and sat quietly. Memories of our training days and all the years we worked together came rushing back. He was very dear to me,” he said.
Meanwhile, the friends and family of the other victims — HS Nataraj (businessman from Huliyurdurga), 
Shankar Gowda
 (advocate from Tumakuru), 
Sudheer
 (advocate from Nagarabhavi in the city), and Bachihalli Pratap Gowda (city-based civil contractor) — are in shock too.
Shankar’s father-in-law Narasimhamurthy said he learnt of the tragedy while watching TV. Shankar, an advocate, lived with his son and wife in Saptagiri Layout, Tumakuru. With tears in his eyes, Narasimhamurthy said: “I was shocked to see the name and details of my son-in-law among the victims of the chopper crash. He had spoken with me last week, saying he was going to Char Dham Yatra.”
Nagesh, a businessman and childhood friend of Nataraj, said the latter had called him around 11am Friday, stating they were sitting inside the chopper, waiting for the weather to clear. “Nataraj explained there was thick fog in the area and their pilot (Himanshu) had told them they would have to wait until the fog cleared,” he said. According to Nagesh, Nataraj and Arun became friends when the latter worked in Huliyurdurga police station, Kunigal.
Dasappa, owner of Arun’s flat in Ramamurthy Nagar, said the late inspector always behaved like a common man. “He was soft-natured, something uncommon in a cop. We cannot believe he is no more,” he said.
Vivek Subbareddy, president of the Advocates’ Association of Bangalore (AAB), said Sudheer and Shankar were practising advocates. “It is a great loss for the advocates’ fraternity... they were supposed to return to Bengaluru from Dehradun Friday night. The family members of the victims will be heading to Joshimath to collect the remains,” he said.
Pratap
Just hours before the tragedy, B Pratap Gowda had spoken to his wife, Dikshitha, reassuring her that he would be back home in Bengaluru by evening. “His last words were that he would board the flight and reach home by 7pm or 8pm,” recalled Prajwal, Dikshitha’s brother.
For the family, the tragedy has not only taken away a loved one but also a man they believed was destined to serve society on a larger platform. “My brother devoted more than a decade of his life to social service in our hometown,” said his cousin Vikram, fighting back tears. Family members recalled that Pratap had even spent money to install a statue of Kempegowda in Sakleshpur, a gesture that reflected his commitment to the community.

briefs.headline: Prison Intelligence: Bengaluru officials step up vigil against contraband and irregularities
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 From monitoring prisoner communications and breaking up long-standing gang networks to transferring suspect staff and quarantining inmates returning from hospitals and court appearances, Karnataka’s prison department is adopting a multi-pronged strategy to curb irregularities and prevent contraband from entering prisons. The new initiative, Prison Intelligence, requires staff to function like law-and-order police, gathering information and taking preventive action.
The measures appear to be yielding results. A four-hour surprise search at Central Prison, Parappana Agrahara, did not uncover a single contraband item, not even tobacco, Friday.
DGP (prison and correctional services) Alok Kumar told 
TOI
 that prison staff had been instructed to go beyond routine duties and actively gather intelligence, conduct basic investigations and monitor inmates’ activities. “Every prisoner should be monitored. The staff should keep watch on which prisoner is communicating with whom, why they are communicating and other such aspects,” Kumar said.
He recalled that around 30 mobile phones had earlier been recovered after being buried 2-3ft underground, necessitating the use of an earthmover. Smuggling attempts remained an everyday challenge, he said, adding that the department’s aim is to make all prisons free of contraband at the earliest.
Prisoners and visitors sometimes allegedly conceal prohibited items in their footwear, while others throw contraband into prison premises from the road. The department is monitoring such activities and seizing the items, Kumar said.
Staff transfers
In another significant measure, the department is ensuring that staff suspected of involvement in offences are not reposted to the same prisons. Around 95% of personnel suspected of involvement in irregularities have been transferred to different prisons, Kumar said.
The department has also moved to break established links among inmates across barracks. Prisoners are being allotted barracks alphabetically, while gangs that had remained together in the same barracks or cells for 15-20 years have been dispersed. The exercise also covers prisoners arrested in terror-related cases, Kumar said.
Five-day quarantine
Prisoners returning from court appearances or hospital visits are kept in quarantine for five days. Kumar said the measure aims to prevent contraband concealed inside the body from being brought into prisons, noting that such items cannot be retained in body cavities for more than 24 hours.
Monitoring has also been strengthened during prisoner escorts. When CAR police take inmates outside prison premises, prison personnel are now deployed in escort vehicles to monitor their communications and act on anything suspicious.
251 cops, four-hour search
The measures were highlighted during Friday’s extensive search at Central Prison, Parappana Agrahara. A team of 251 police personnel, led by Electronics City DCP M Narayana, entered the prison around 7am and completed the operation by 11am.
The team thoroughly searched barracks housing undertrials and convicted prisoners, including the women’s barrack, but found no contraband.
A senior officer said access between barracks housing convicted prisoners, undertrials, women prisoners and inmates in high-security sections had been restricted. Barricades had been installed to prevent inmates from moving freely between barracks. Regular surprise checks were also being conducted to strengthen security.

stories.headline: Government extends import duty exemption for cotton
stories.deck: In a notification issued on October 30, the Finance Ministry said the exemption, which had been granted in May this year, will continue until October 31
stories.bodyText:
The Finance Ministry extended the import duty on cotton until December 31, 2026, providing relief to the largest cotton consumer—the textile industry.
In a notification issued on Friday, October 30, 2026, the Finance Ministry said the exemption, which had been granted in May this year, will continue until October 31. The exemption will now extend to the end of December.
With the poor Southwest monsoon impacting the cotton crop, daily arrivals of cotton remain low, though the new cotton marketing season began on October 1. The textile industry, meanwhile, expects cotton consumption to increase this year. The textile industry has been demanding the removal of the import duty on cotton.

stories.headline: 'Play only administrative role in NCLT appointment'
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: A day after Supreme Court's observation on the role of 
ministry of corporate affairs
 in the appointment and infrastructure in the National Company Law Tribunal and the appellate tribunal, the ministry on Friday said it only performed "administrative" role in conducting the appointment process for the 63 judicial and technical members of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)
"NCLT independently undertakes the process for appointment and management of its officers and staff, including deputy registrars, court officers, stenographers, office assistants and multi-tasking staff," MCA said in a statement.
In Oct 2019, govt delegated the responsibility to NCLT to ensure its effective and independent functioning, govt added. On Thursday, SC slammed the ministry for "completely hijacking" both NCLT and NCLAT, while hearing a petition regarding the dilapidated infrastructure, lack of support staff and vacancies, hampering the work in the tribunal that deals with corporate law and insolvency cases.

stories.headline: Sebi relaxes timeline for FPI KYC updates
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: To simplify the compliance process for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) registered in India, markets regulator Sebi on Friday extended the periodicity of Know Your Client (KYC) review from one year at present to eight years.
"Currently, FPIs are subject to periodic KYC review annually or once every three years, depending on the applicable category and other criteria. The revised framework increases the periodicity from one year to two years and from three years to eight years," a Sebi circular said. For some special category of FPI labelled under Swagat-FIs, "the periodicity of KYC review will remain unchanged at 10 years. Also, the existing relaxations for GS-FPIs will remain unchanged," the circular said.

stories.headline: India orders Sun Pharma to halt eye-care drug production at plant after quality lapses
stories.deck: India’s drug quality standards have come under increased scrutiny at home and overseas in recent years after locally made cough syrups were linked to ‌the deaths of children in India and also in countries including Gambia and Uzbekistan
stories.bodyText:
Indian drug regulators ordered Sun Pharmaceutical Industries to stop manufacturing, selling and distributing ophthalmic products made at its Assam facility after finding failure in its quality management system, documents reviewed by Reuters showed.
The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation and the office of Drugs Controller Assam ordered the shutdown on August 20 after a joint federal-state inspection of the facility identified lapses in the system meant to ensure product quality and safety, following Sun Pharma’s move in July to voluntarily recall about 11 eye-care brands.
India’s drug quality standards have come under increased scrutiny at home and overseas in recent years after locally made cough syrups were linked to the deaths of children in India and also in countries including Gambia and Uzbekistan.
The regulatory agencies’ move marks an escalation of the action against Sun Pharma, India’s biggest pharmaceutical firm, which will be unable to continue ophthalmic drug production at the Assam factory until it submits a satisfactory compliance report. Sun Pharma said previously the site was expected to become one of its largest manufacturing hubs for sterile products in a business identified as a key global growth driver.
The regulator sought more information on the recall of 332 batches of ophthalmic suspension products — liquids used to treat eye conditions — the documents showed.
In an internal notice sent to stockists at the time, the company said it was withdrawing the products as a “precautionary measure.” It remains unclear whether all of the recalled products were contaminated.
Sun Pharma did not publicly disclose details of the recall.
The company has submitted a compliance report in response to the order, which is being reviewed by the regulator, an official familiar with the matter told Reuters on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
“We voluntarily initiated a temporary cessation of manufacturing activities and informed the regulators,” Sun Pharma said in a statement on Friday (October 30, 2026), adding that remedial measures have been put in place.
It did not respond to a request for comment on the recall. The company says on its website it follows a single global quality standard.
Recall could involve hundreds of thousands of bottles
Some of the recalled products included Lotepred 1% 5ml eye drops, Nepalact OD eye drops, Nepalact-Z, Brinzotim eye drops 5ml and Depopred 2ml. The eye drops are used to treat eye inflammation, infections and chronic eye diseases, according to doctors.
It is unclear whether these eye products were exported from India or whether any patients reported any adverse effects.
Reuters found that, based on the product packaging, most of the recalled products were manufactured at the Assam state facility in Kokjhar village. Reuters could not independently verify whether the 332 batches cited by regulators were related only to the 11 identified brands in the recall notice or included additional brands.
The affected batches could translate into hundreds of thousands of eye-drop bottles, according to industry experts, who declined to be identified because they were not authorised to speak publicly.
Ophthalmology contributes about 3% of Sun Pharma’s domestic revenue, according to its 2025-26 annual report. It is also one of its key areas for the U.S.
The company reported a drop in second-quarter profit on Friday (October 30) weighed down by a one-time charge related to its acquisition of U.S.-based Organon.
The eye product recall coincided with a patient-safety advisory issued in June by the All India Ophthalmological Society (AIOS), an independent body of eye specialists, warning that certain batches of Predmet eye drops appeared to be contaminated.
“There were some adverse cases of infections reported in patients who used Predmet and we got sealed bottles investigated and found it was contaminated,” Santosh Honavar, a doctor and secretary of AIOS, told Reuters, adding that Sun Pharma had also recalled those Predmet drops.
Sun Pharma did not respond a request for comment on the AIOS advisory.
The regulators issued a show-cause notice to Sun Pharma on August 10, citing the quality management system failures, the documents showed.
Dissatisfied with the company’s response, the regulators ordered a halt to the manufacturing, sale and distribution of all ophthalmic products from the facility.
Indian regulators did not respond to requests for comment. The agency did not issue a public health alert after the recall.
It is not the first time Sun Pharma’s sterile manufacturing facilities have faced regulatory scrutiny. Last year, the U.S. FDA halted the company’s shipments from Gujarat’s Halol plant after inspectors cited shortcomings in contamination controls.
